paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The most considerable of the confederacies of antiquity was that of the Grecian republics, joined together under the Amphictyonic Council. By the best accounts we have of this celebrated institution, it closely resembled the present Confederation of the American States, and the resemblance is very instructive.

The members kept the character of independent and sovereign states, and each had an equal vote in the federal council. The council had general authority to propose and decide whatever it judged necessary for the common welfare of Greece. It could declare and wage war, decide all controversies between the members in the last resort, fine the aggressing party, turn the whole force of the confederacy against the disobedient, and admit new members. The Amphictyons were the guardians of religion and of the immense riches that belonged to the temple of Delphos. There they had the right of jurisdiction in controversies between the inhabitants and those who came to consult the oracle. To give the federal powers further effectiveness, the Amphictyons swore an oath to defend and protect the united cities mutually, to punish anyone who violated the oath, and to take vengeance on sacrilegious despoilers of the temple.

In theory, and on paper, this array of powers seems amply sufficient for all general purposes. In several important respects it goes beyond the powers listed in the Articles of Confederation. The Amphictyons controlled the superstition of the times, which was one of the principal engines by which government was then maintained. They also had a declared authority to use coercion against refractory cities, and an oath bound them to use it when the occasion required.

The experiment, nevertheless, turned out very differently from the theory. As in the present Congress, the powers were administered by deputies appointed wholly by the cities in their political capacities, and they were exercised over the cities in those same capacities. From this came the weakness, the disorders, and finally the destruction of the confederacy. The more powerful members, instead of being held in awe and subordination, tyrannized in turn over all the rest. Athens, as we learn from Demosthenes, was the arbiter of Greece for seventy-three years. The Lacedaemonians governed it next, for twenty-nine years. At a later time, after the battle of Leuctra, the Thebans had their turn at domination.
Plutarch tells us it happened all too often that the deputies of the strongest cities overawed and corrupted those of the weaker ones, and that judgment went to the most powerful party.

Even in the midst of defensive and dangerous wars with Persia and Macedon, the members never acted together. More or fewer of them were always the dupes or the hirelings of the common enemy. The intervals between foreign wars were filled with domestic upheavals, convulsions, and carnage.

After the war with Xerxes ended, the Lacedaemonians, it appears, demanded that a number of the cities be expelled from the confederacy for the unfaithful part they had played. The Athenians saw that the Lacedaemonians would lose fewer partisans by this measure than they themselves would, and would become masters of the public deliberations. They therefore opposed the attempt vigorously and defeated it. This piece of history proves at once the ineffectiveness of the union, the ambition and jealousy of its most powerful members, and the dependent and degraded condition of the rest. By the theory of their system the smaller members were entitled to revolve in equal pride and majesty around the common center. In fact they had become satellites of the orbs of primary magnitude.

The Abbe Milot says that if the Greeks had been as wise as they were courageous, experience would have taught them the need of a closer union. They would have used the peace that followed their success against the Persian arms to make that reform. Instead of this obvious policy, Athens and Sparta, puffed up with the victories and glory they had won, became first rivals and then enemies. They did each other infinitely more harm than they had suffered from Xerxes. Their mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries ended in the celebrated Peloponnesian war, which in turn ended in the ruin and slavery of the Athenians who had started it.

A weak government that is not at war is always agitated by internal dissensions, and these never fail to bring fresh calamities from abroad. The Phocians had plowed up some consecrated ground belonging to the temple of Apollo. In keeping with the superstition of the age, the Amphictyonic Council fined the sacrilegious offenders. The Phocians, supported by Athens and Sparta, refused to submit to the decree. The Thebans, with some of the other cities, undertook to maintain the authority of the Amphictyons and to avenge the violated god. Because the Thebans were the weaker party, they invited the assistance of Philip of Macedon, who had secretly stirred up the quarrel. Philip gladly seized the chance to carry out the designs against the liberties of Greece that he had long planned. By his intrigues and bribes he won over the popular leaders of several cities. Through their influence and votes he gained admission to the Amphictyonic Council. And through his arts and his arms he made himself master of the confederacy.

These were the consequences of the fallacious principle on which this interesting establishment was founded. A judicious observer, writing on the fate of Greece, says that if she had been united by a stricter confederation and had held to her union, she would never have worn the chains of Macedon. She might even have proved a barrier to the vast projects of Rome.
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another society of Grecian republics, and it gives us valuable instruction.

Here the union was far closer, and the organization much wiser, than in the previous case. It will therefore appear that, though the league did not escape a similar catastrophe, it by no means deserved it as much.

The cities that made up this league kept their municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, held the sole and exclusive right of peace and war, of sending and receiving ambassadors, and of entering into treaties and alliances. It also appointed a chief executive, called the praetor, who commanded their armies. With the advice and consent of ten of the senators, the praetor not only administered the government while the senate was in recess but also had a great share in its deliberations when it was in session. Under the original constitution two praetors shared the administration, but after a trial a single one was preferred.

It appears that all the cities had the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money. How far this came from the authority of the federal council, however, is left uncertain. We are told only that the cities were in a manner compelled to accept the same laws and usages. When Philopoemen brought Lacedaemon into the league, the institutions and laws of Lycurgus were abolished and those of the Achaeans adopted. The Amphictyonic confederacy, of which she had been a member, had left her in full exercise of her government and her legislation. This circumstance alone proves a very important difference in the character of the two systems.

It is much to be regretted that such imperfect records survive of this curious political structure. If we could determine its internal structure and regular operation, it would probably throw more light on the science of federal government than any of the similar experiments known to us.

All the historians who notice Achaean affairs seem to attest one important fact. After the league was renewed by Aratus, as before it was dissolved by the arts of Macedon, its government was administered with infinitely more moderation and justice, and its people showed less violence and sedition, than could be found in any of the cities that exercised SINGLY all the prerogatives of sovereignty. The Abbe Mably, in his observations on Greece, says that the popular government, so tempestuous elsewhere, caused no disorders among the members of the Achaean republic, BECAUSE IT WAS THERE TEMPERED BY THE GENERAL AUTHORITY AND LAWS OF THE CONFEDERACY.

We must not conclude too hastily, however, that faction did not to some degree agitate the particular cities, much less that proper subordination and harmony reigned in the general system. The ups and downs and the fate of the republic show the contrary clearly enough.

While the Amphictyonic confederacy lasted, the Achaean confederacy, which included only the less important cities, made little figure on the stage of Greece. When the former fell victim to Macedon, the latter was spared by the policy of Philip and Alexander. Under the successors of these princes, however, a different policy prevailed. The arts of division were practiced among the Achaeans. Each city was seduced into a separate interest, and the union was dissolved. Some of the cities fell under the tyranny of Macedonian garrisons, others under that of usurpers who rose out of their own confusion. Shame and oppression soon awakened their love of liberty. A few cities reunited, and others followed their example as chances arose to get rid of their tyrants. The league soon took in almost the whole Peloponnesus. Macedon saw its progress but was kept by internal dissensions from stopping it. All Greece caught the enthusiasm and seemed ready to unite in one confederacy. Then the jealousy and envy that Sparta and Athens felt at the rising glory of the Achaeans threw a fatal damper on the enterprise. Fear of the Macedonian power led the league to court the alliance of the Kings of Egypt and Syria, who as successors of Alexander were rivals of the king of Macedon. Cleomenes, king of Sparta, defeated this policy. His ambition led him to make an unprovoked attack on his neighbors the Achaeans, and as an enemy of Macedon he had enough influence with the Egyptian and Syrian princes to make them break their engagements with the league.

The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or begging aid from Macedon, their former oppressor. They chose the latter. The contests of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a welcome chance to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly appeared and Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon learned, as so often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is only another name for a master. All that their most abject compliance could win from him was toleration of the exercise of their laws. Philip, now on the throne of Macedon, soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks by his tyrannies. The Achaeans were weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members. Even so, they joined the AEtolians and Athenians and raised the standard of opposition. Finding themselves unequal to the undertaking even with this support, they once more resorted to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, to whom the invitation was made, eagerly accepted it. Philip was conquered and Macedon subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members, and the Romans encouraged them. Callicrates and other popular leaders became paid instruments for luring their countrymen astray. To feed discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans had already proclaimed universal liberty(1) throughout Greece, to the astonishment of those who trusted their sincerity. With the same treacherous aims, they now drew the members away from the league by appealing to their pride over the violation it committed on their sovereignty. By these arts this union, the last hope of Greece, the last hope of ancient liberty, was torn to pieces. Such weakness and distraction were introduced that the arms of Rome found little difficulty in completing the ruin their arts had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia was loaded with chains, under which it groans to this hour.

I have thought it not superfluous to give the outlines of this important portion of history, both because it teaches more than one lesson and because it adds to the outline of the Achaean constitution. It emphatically illustrates the tendency of federal bodies to produce anarchy among the members rather than tyranny in the head.
1. This was only a more plausible-sounding name for the independence of the members from the federal head.
